clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathy that is clinically indistinguishable from other CMT1 subtypes, so genetic testing is required to confirm the LITAF cause.
Presents as a length-dependent motor and sensory neuropathy with distal weakness, pes cavus, hammer toes, distal wasting and lost ankle reflexes.
Motor nerve conduction velocities are uniformly slowed into the demyelinating range across multiple nerves, mirroring CMT1A and CMT1B.
Onset is usually within the first two decades but later presentation occurs; progression is characteristically slow.
Caused by mutations in LITAF (also called SIMPLE), which disrupt endosomal-lysosomal protein handling within Schwann cells.
Sural nerve biopsy, when performed, shows demyelination with remyelination and onion-bulb formation.
Consider this subtype when PMP22 dosage and MPZ testing are negative in a dominant demyelinating pedigree.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1C is caused by heterozygous mutations in LITAF (lipopolysaccharide-induced tumour necrosis factor factor), whose product is also known as SIMPLE (small integral membrane protein of the lysosome and late endosome). The protein participates in endosomal protein sorting and degradation, interacting with the endosomal sorting complex required for transport machinery that regulates trafficking and turnover of membrane proteins. Disease-associated missense changes cluster in the conserved membrane-associated domain and promote protein misfolding and aggregation, impairing Schwann cell handling of myelin and receptor proteins. The resulting Schwann cell dysfunction produces a chronic demyelinating and remyelinating process with onion-bulb formation, secondary axonal loss and the uniform conduction slowing typical of the CMT1 group.
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm uniform demyelinating slowing
PMP22 dosage analysis (MLPA) to exclude CMT1A duplication
Next-generation sequencing hereditary neuropathy gene panel including LITAF
Sural nerve biopsy reserved for diagnostically unclear cases
Orthopaedic and podiatric assessment of foot deformity and gait
redFlags: Rapid progression or marked asymmetry suggesting an acquired inflammatory neuropathy
Prominent sensory ataxia out of keeping with the motor picture
Conduction block on studies favouring an acquired demyelinating process
reference.prognosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1C is slowly progressive with a normal life expectancy, and independent ambulation is usually preserved into adulthood although foot deformity and distal weakness accrue over time.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the demyelinating slowing as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy and giving unnecessary immunotherapy.
Assuming CMT1A without performing PMP22 dosage testing.
Overlooking a subtle dominant family history in an apparently isolated case.
Attributing foot deformity to an orthopaedic cause and missing the underlying neuropathy.
references: Charcot-Marie-Tooth hereditary neuropathy overview (clinical genetics reference)
Adams and Victor's principles of neurology
management: Manage supportively with physiotherapy and occupational therapy, as no disease-modifying drug is available
Fit ankle-foot orthoses and provide podiatry, footwear and walking aids for foot drop and pes cavus
Offer orthopaedic foot surgery for fixed, disabling deformity and gait problems
Treat neuropathic pain and cramps symptomatically and avoid neurotoxic agents such as vincristine
Monitor the slow progression with periodic neurological and functional assessment, including screening for scoliosis
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and family segregation testing for the LITAF variant
Coordinate multidisciplinary neuromuscular, orthopaedic and rehabilitation care
